name: PT Graha Andrasentra Propertindo Tbk

frontmatter.title: JungleLand: a Bogor park and hotel, and an appraised land bank under the equity
frontmatter.summary: A loss-making Bogor park and hotel sitting on IDR922.9bn of land for development, IDR765.8bn of it independently appraised in May 2025 and none of it pledged. On cash flow alone the equity is worth less than nothing; the land is why it is worth more than the price. Rating BUY, target Rp44.
thesis: The operating business does not cover its cost of capital: FY2025 EBIT was IDR7.8bn against IDR10.2bn of finance charges, free cash flow was negative (IDR-5.9bn) and nine-month 2026 revenue of IDR102.4bn against IDR107.3bn carried an operating loss of IDR4.1bn [S6 p14][S7 p7].

The land is appraised, not historical cost: land for development is IDR922.9bn against IDR1,518.2bn of total assets and IDR1,088.1bn of book equity, and IDR765.8bn of the line is a May-2025 independent appraisal (KJPP Febriman Siregar, 2 May 2025) taken in the GTA business combination [S6 note 5 p47][S6 note 14].

The land is unencumbered: the land-for-development note states that no land for development was used as collateral for any obligation. What is pledged is the operating land and buildings and the inventory, not the development asset [S6 note 14 p58][S6 note 12 p57][S6 note 9 p52].
The market is not paying for it: a market capitalisation of IDR767.8bn is below the carrying value of the land line of IDR922.9bn, before any deduction for net debt [S0][S6].

The governance is the risk, not the asset: PT Surya Global Nusantara is controller with PT Bakrieland Development Tbk as ultimate beneficial owner, and IDR48.6bn is due to related parties on non-interest-bearing, unsecured terms [S8 p54][S7 p5][S6 note 31].
What moves the value is a sale or joint development of the 249 ha Jonggol bank, a hotel recovery, or a refinancing of the related-party balance into third-party debt.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited statements: the segment note, the land-for-development note, the auditor opinion and any movement in the related-party balances we re-underwrite.
FY2026 annual report: the land note, the beneficial-ownership disclosure and any change in the collateral list.
AGM and FY2026 annual report: the first window in which a dividend or a rights issue after three loss years would signal a change in the capital-allocation stance.

blocks.text: Rating BUY, twelve-month target Rp44 against a last price of Rp34, an expected return of 30.3% [S0]. The target is a weighted blend of an FCFF DCF (61%), an EV/EBITDA cross-check (28%) and an EV/Sales cross-check (11%); the P/E leg is dropped because the earnings base is negative [S0][S6]. The DCF values the operating business at IDR100.0bn of enterprise value, below the net debt the latest balance sheet shows, and the land is added in the valuation bridge at carrying value. Every leg is disclosed unfloored in the valuation section: the DCF leg is Rp37 a share and the EV/EBITDA leg Rp40, both positive only because the land bridge lifts equity above the debt line.

The single change from the previous version of this report is the land. Land for development is carried at IDR922.9bn, of which IDR765.8bn came in at fair value in the GTA business combination, measured by an independent appraiser (KJPP Febriman Siregar, report dated 2 May 2025) [S6 note 5 p47]. It is not historical certificate cost, and the previous version was wrong to say it was unappraised. The line is also expressly unencumbered: the land-for-development note says no land for development was used as collateral for any obligation, and the pledged assets are the operating land, buildings and inventory [S6 note 14 p58][S6 note 12 p57][S6 note 9 p52]. The land now enters the valuation bridge at carrying value and sits in all three scenarios.

Without that asset the equity is worthless on the cash flows: the DCF enterprise value is below net debt, so a cash-flow-only valuation would floor at zero. That is the honest arithmetic of a business earning IDR26.4bn of EBITDA in FY2025, spending IDR10.6bn of capex against IDR18.6bn of depreciation, and carrying finance charges of IDR10.2bn [S6 p14/p16/p77]. The land is what makes the equity worth anything, and the market currently pays IDR767.8bn for the whole company.

Indonesian mid-cap leisure and property groups often hold the operating assets and the development land in separate vehicles, and the land can sit at a transaction or cost value well below what neighbouring plots fetch. The statutory accounts do not mark land up annually, and there is no obligation to sell it. Where the operating subsidiary is loss-making, the consolidated accounts show a parent loss while the asset book stands, and the discount of market value to book is a market judgement about whether the asset will ever be monetised rather than about whether it exists. A controlling shareholder with other interests can also direct the balance sheet, which is why the related-party line matters as much as the asset line.

The variant view is that this is an asset story with an operating tail, not a distressed operating story with a land option. Three things move the value. First, the land: IDR922.9bn of carrying value against a market capitalisation of IDR767.8bn, held through PT Gili Tirta Anugerah (249 ha at Jonggol) and unpledged [S8 p62][S6 note 14]. Second, the hotel: the 76.1%-gross-margin segment and the only part of the group with operating leverage to a recovery. Third, the balance sheet: the September 2026 accounts show total liabilities of IDR428.1bn, a related-party balance of IDR48.6bn, and nine-month revenue of IDR102.4bn against IDR107.3bn with an operating loss of IDR4.1bn [S7 p5/p7]. The group is cash-consumptive at the operating level and levered, so the discount rate matters far more than the growth rate.

The company is a single-site leisure operator in Bogor, West Java, running a resort hotel and condotel business, a recreation park and a small real-estate arm, with a land bank held for development [S6 note 25][S8]. FY2025 revenue of IDR155.8bn split into hotel and condotel of IDR82.6bn, recreation park of IDR54.7bn and real estate of IDR7.6bn, with the balance in other services [S6 p69]. The mix matters because the margins differ sharply: hotel and condotel earned 76.1% and the recreation park 64.4% in FY2025, the park down from a materially higher level a year earlier on the Bogor minimum-wage rise, higher repairs and utility costs [S8 p65-66].

The recreation park is the identity of the group. The Jungle Waterpark holds a Top Brand Award for water parks [S4], and a JungleSea project is planned in Lampung but is not built [S5]. The claim that the group operates the second-largest theme park in Indonesia does not belong to it: the press profile that makes the claim is describing PT Jungleland Asia, the associate in which the group holds 38.1% and whose carrying value has been written to zero [S5][S6 p54]. The group's own park is a strong local brand in the Bogor catchment, not a national number two. The hotel is a single Aston-branded resort at the same Bogor site, with condotel units operated alongside the hotel rooms [S5][S8]. The real-estate arm markets apartments at the site, with 489 J.Sky units across the Azure and Balfour wings [S8 p62], and a subsidiary, PT Gili Tirta Anugerah, holds a land bank of 249 ha at Jonggol [S8 p62]. The group employs 425 people, a small headcount for the asset base because the hotel is managed and the park is seasonal [S8 p50].

The balance sheet is where this company differs from a normal leisure operator. Land for development stood at IDR922.9bn at end-2025 against IDR1,518.2bn of total assets and IDR1,088.1bn of book equity, having risen from a small fraction of that a year earlier when a non-current receivable was converted into land [S6 note 14]. The IDR765.8bn GTA portion was measured at fair value by an independent appraiser in May 2025, so the largest single asset on the balance sheet carries a 2025 valuation, not original certificate cost [S6 note 5 p47]. The line is not pledged [S6 p58]. It is the main support for a book value per share of Rp48 against a share price of Rp34 [S6][S0]. Fixed assets of IDR382.9bn carry the park, the hotel and the condotel, and are depreciated at IDR18.6bn a year against capex of IDR10.6bn [S6 p16/p77].

PT Surya Global Nusantara is the controlling shareholder, with PT Bakrieland Development Tbk named as the ultimate beneficiary owner in the annual report [S8 p54]; the general-affairs note in the accounts describes Surya Global Nusantara as the parent and Bakrieland as the ultimate parent [S8 p203]. Free float is 33.5% against insiders at 52.1% [S0]. The strategy disclosed in the annual report is cost control and completion of the existing park, hotel and condotel pipeline rather than expansion [S8]. There is an associate, PT Jungleland Asia, at 38.1% after dilution, which generated IDR27.9bn of revenue and a net loss of IDR231.6bn in FY2025, of which the group booked IDR46.6bn [S6 p14/p54][S8 p55]. The carrying value was written to zero and no equity-method loss appears in the nine-month 2026 accounts [S6][S7].

Position: leader at its own site in the Bogor catchment, challenger nationally. The park's local monopoly is real but the catchment is finite, and the hotel competes with a large Bogor-Puncak-Cianjur resort stock. The group has no second operating site, no management contract for a third party and no franchise that would let it export the park brand, so growth has to come from the same gates and the same rooms [S8].

The leisure industry in Indonesia is a domestic-demand business: park and hotel revenue is a function of household discretionary spending in the Greater Jakarta catchment, school-holiday calendars and long weekends, and it is not export-priced [S8]. Growth is tied to the middle-income consumer rather than to any commodity or currency cycle; the drivers for this industry sit in the macro deck, not in a commodity price [S0]. The demand base is deep but seasonal: weekends, Idul Fitri, Christmas and the school holidays carry the park, and the hotel depends on the same calendar plus corporate meetings and domestic government travel [S8].

The competitive set is fragmented. Bogor, Puncak and Cianjur hold a large stock of villas, resorts and glamping sites, and the water-park format is replicated across Greater Jakarta at lower price points; the group's advantage is location, brand recognition from the Top Brand award and the combination of a hotel and a park on one ticket [S4][S8]. There is no disclosed market-share figure in the filings, so we treat the position as a strong local brand rather than a measured leader.

Regulation that matters here is local: minimum-wage decisions (the Bogor minimum-wage rise is cited in the FY2025 gross-margin decline of the park), building and safety permits for rides and attractions, and sharia-compliant financing structures such as Musyarakah, which the group uses for part of its debt [S8][S6 p12]. Tourism policy at the national level is supportive in principle but the filings disclose no licence, concession or subsidy that would change the group's revenue line [S8].

Competitive position: the recreation park has a genuine moat at its own location, evidenced by the Top Brand award and a 64.4% gross margin [S4][S8 p66], but the moat does not travel: the Lampung project is a plan, not a build. The hotel is a single property under a management contract with no brand power of its own. The five forces are unfavourable on buyer power (price-sensitive domestic day-trippers who can substitute a mall or a free public park), neutral on supplier power (payroll and utilities are the main inputs, and the park is a price-taker on both), weak on new entrants (land and permits are the barrier, which is exactly the asset the group holds) and adverse on substitutes (domestic travel destinations, malls, streaming and short-haul overseas trips).

External influences: rupiah financing cost, minimum-wage inflation, and the land-value environment around Bogor. The first two are in the model through the cost of debt and the opex ratio; the third is not in the earnings forecast at all, which is precisely the gap between the cash-flow value and the book value discussed in the valuation section. None of these is a company-specific source of upside today [S8][S6].

Theme parks are a fixed-cost business with a hard capacity ceiling: once the gates, rides and car parks are built, incremental visitors cost very little to serve, so margins swing sharply with attendance, and attendance swings with the household budget and the weather. The same is true of a single resort hotel, where rooms are fixed and the marginal cost of an occupied night is low. That operating leverage is why the park margin fell when the Bogor wage floor rose, and why a small revenue recovery would lift EBITDA disproportionately. It is also why a revenue decline of the size the nine-month accounts show is more damaging than the same decline would be for a distributor.

The land is the second industry fact that matters. Bogor's southern corridor has been a development frontier for two decades, and land held since the original acquisition can sit in the accounts at a small fraction of the price at which neighbouring plots trade. Here the position is better than that: the GTA land was brought in at an appraised value, and the whole development line is unpledged, so the asset is both valued and available to the equity [S6 note 5/14][S8 p62]. What the filings do not give is a selling price, a buyer or a development timetable, so this report carries the land at carrying value in the valuation bridge and adds no development margin: the option to develop is real, but its exercise requires a corporate decision that has not been announced.

Revenue fell -5.9% in FY2025 to IDR155.8bn, and we forecast -5.0% in FY2026E to IDR148.0bn, then flat in FY2027E and 2.0% to 3.0% thereafter [S6][S7][S8]. Gross margin is held at the FY2025 actual of 64.7% in FY2026E and expands from 64.7% to 66.5% by FY2030E as the 76.1% hotel segment recovers share from the 64.4% park [S6 p14][S8 p65-66]. Total operating expenses were IDR93.0bn in FY2025. We do not hold the FY2025 annual ratio of 62.7% blind to the nine-month evidence: the 2026 LK shows operating expenses of IDR74.9bn on revenue of IDR102.4bn, and although Q4 is the seasonally light-cost quarter, a full year lands near 62.7% rather than at the FY2025 average. The ratio falls to 60.0% by FY2030E as the same fixed cost base spreads over a recovering top line [S6 p14][S7 p7][S8 p67].

The forecast against the nine months that are already actual: nine-month revenue of IDR102.4bn carried gross profit of IDR70.8bn and an operating loss of IDR4.1bn [S7 p7]. FY2026E of IDR148.0bn with EBITDA of IDR20.7bn therefore assumes a fourth quarter at the prior year's seasonal strength, which is the historical pattern: Q4 2025 carried almost all of the year's operating profit, as the nine-month 2025 figure of IDR0.5bn against FY2025 operating profit of IDR7.8bn shows, on a third of its revenue [S7 p7][S6 p14]. The corrected seasonality strengthens rather than weakens the FY2026E assumption. If Q4 disappoints, FY2026 EBITDA undershoots and the DCF enterprise value falls; that is the bear case.

Restatement note, material to every number above: the data pack overstates FY2025 operating profit and understates interest. The pack shows a materially higher operating profit and a lower operating expense than the audited statements, which show operating profit of IDR7.8bn on total operating expenses of IDR93.0bn, the gap being a selling-expense line the pack omits [S6 p14]. The pack interest expense is the cash component only; the statement line "Beban bunga dan keuangan" is IDR10.2bn including Musyarakah and lease finance charges, against cash interest paid of IDR10.5bn [S6 p14/p16]. We restate both from the LK, which is why FY2025 EBITDA is IDR26.4bn and not the pack figure, and why interest cover is thin. Land for development was IDR922.9bn, the largest item on the balance sheet, rising from a small fraction of that as a receivable was converted to land; the operating cash flow was IDR4.1bn [S6 note 14][S6 p16]. One historical artefact to flag: the model's FY2024 free cash flow is inflated by a non-cash working-capital movement when the GTA receivable was converted into land, so the FY2024 line is not operating cash flow and we do not anchor any forecast on it [S6 note 5/14].
Earnings-quality flags from the house card:

items: Accruals ratio: net profit of IDR-46.4bn against operating cash flow of IDR4.1bn on average total assets of about IDR1,518.2bn is deeply negative, i.e. cash profit is not the problem; the loss is real and is driven by the associate write-down [S0][S6]. FY2024 is similarly negative.
Cash conversion: operating cash flow of IDR4.1bn against EBITDA of IDR26.4bn is poor; working capital absorbed IDR21.7bn in FY2025 on real-estate inventory [S0][S6].

IDX regime: no special-monitoring-board status or notation letter (B/E/L/M/S) is disclosed for the company; the first three quarters are unaudited, so the nine-month figures carry fourth-quarter true-up risk [S7].

Related-party gravity: IDR48.1bn due to related parties at end-2025, IDR48.6bn at the September 2026 balance date, against IDR155.8bn of revenue and IDR428.1bn of total liabilities [S6 p12][S7 p5]. The balance is non-interest-bearing and unsecured per the related-party note; we found no guarantee to group ventures in it, and the previous version's claim that one was disclosed is withdrawn [S6 note 31].

Structure flags: no pledge of the controlling shareholding is disclosed. The operating land and buildings are pledged to the bank and Musyarakah facilities, and the inventory is pledged for the Musyarakah financing, but the land for development is expressly not pledged [S6 p57/p52/p58]. No rights issue or discounted private placement to affiliates is disclosed in the period [S3][S7]. Auditor and opinion are unchanged.

blocks.text: Balance sheet and debt: at 31 December 2025 cash of IDR15.7bn against debt of IDR211.5bn gave net debt of IDR195.8bn, 7.4x EBITDA, with IDR75.1bn of bank loans and IDR53.7bn of Musyarakah financing in the non-current mix [S6 p12]. That is the FY2025 statement position. The valuation is struck on the later, 30 September 2026 balance sheet, where total liabilities were IDR428.1bn and the related-party balance IDR48.6bn; the bank, Musyarakah and lease facilities remain outstanding and cash has fallen since the year-end. Interest-bearing debt at that date also includes a IDR69.7bn long-term other payable to PT Lumbung Teknologi Envirotama, which the long-term other payables note describes as a working-capital loan at 10.0% per annum maturing 23 September 2028 [S7 p5][S7 p50]. Our debt definition is interest-bearing borrowings only — bank loans, Musyarakah financing, lease/asset-purchase liabilities and that LTE loan — the same definition the FY2025 debt line of IDR211.5bn uses. The IDR48.6bn due to related parties is contractually non-interest-bearing and unsecured and sits outside net debt; including it would raise net debt by that balance [S7 p5][S6 note 31]. Total liabilities at end-2025 were IDR429.7bn against IDR1,518.2bn of assets [S6 p13]. Equity is IDR1,088.1bn, of which the land-for-development line is IDR922.9bn and fixed assets IDR382.9bn [S6 note 14][S0]. Capital allocation: no dividend in any year of history and a nil payout, capex of IDR10.6bn against depreciation of IDR18.6bn, i.e. the asset base is being consumed rather than renewed [S0][S6 p16/p77].

Method set: FCFF DCF as primary, EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales as market cross-checks, with P/E dropped because FY2025 earnings are negative and the LTM metric is unusable. The weights are 61% DCF, 28% EV/EBITDA and 11% EV/Sales after the P/E leg drops out; the revenue multiple is included precisely because, at the 64.7% gross margin, revenue is the one line that remains positive and comparable across a park and a hotel. A P/BV leg is deliberately excluded, but for a different reason than the previous version gave: the book is not historical-cost land, it is an appraised land bank, so applying a peer P/BV would apply an operating-business multiple to a single appraised asset and double-count the question. The land is valued directly in the valuation bridge instead.
WACC and cost-of-equity build-up:

The cost of equity of 13.1% is built as the risk-free rate of 7.4% less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6%, plus a levered beta of 1.09 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. The default-spread subtraction is the term the previous version omitted; without it the build-up does not reconcile. The pre-tax market cost of debt of 9.4% sits above the 5.5% blended cash rate the company actually pays, because the related-party balance is contractually non-interest-bearing [S7 p5][S6 note 31]. WACC is 11.9%, inside the house IDR band.
Primary method:

The DCF values the operating business at IDR100.0bn of enterprise value, with 36.7% in the terminal value on terminal growth of 3.0% [S0]. That enterprise value is below the net debt on the latest balance sheet, so the operating business on its own is worth less than its debt and the equity would floor at zero without the land. The land is added in the valuation bridge at IDR922.9bn of carrying value, of which IDR765.8bn is the May-2025 independent appraisal; it generates none of the forecast cash flow, so it cannot sit inside the enterprise value, and adding it once to equity is the correct treatment [S6 note 5/14].

Each leg, unfloored and weighted: the DCF produces Rp37 a share at a 61% weight; EV/EBITDA at 6.5x on restated LTM EBITDA of IDR26.4bn produces Rp40 at 28%; EV/Sales at 2.5x produces Rp50 at 11% [S0]. The DCF and EV/EBITDA legs are floored at zero in isolation, but with the land bridge they contribute positively; the EV/Sales leg is the most generous and sits 35.4% above the DCF; we hold its weight at the bottom of the three for that reason. The blended value before the twelve-month roll is Rp39. The target that results — the numbers used for the rating — incorporates the land and is not solely an arithmetic floor.
Cross-checks and divergences:

The divergence that matters is not between methods but between the operating value and the asset value. The operating business is worth between IDR100.0bn of enterprise value on the DCF and the 6.5x peer multiple on LTM EBITDA; the land is worth IDR922.9bn at carrying value. The equity is the operating value plus the land less net debt, and the market at IDR767.8bn is paying close to the land line net of interest-bearing debt, so the parks, hotel and condotel are being ascribed little or no value. We do not resolve that gap by inventing a development margin: the land is carried at its appraised and book value, and the option to develop it is not priced.

The compounder-quality card, tested on its output contract: reinvestment is negative. FY2026E capex of IDR10.4bn is below the D&A charge of IDR17.8bn, working capital is held at 24.0% of revenue so there is no build, and net investment is therefore a release rather than a use. Because incremental invested capital is negative, a reinvestment rate (net investment over NOPAT) and an incremental ROIC are not meaningful for this name: the card is built for businesses that compound capital, and this one is harvesting an asset base, which is why the DCF is a declining-cash-flow value even though revenue rises. The return that does matter is the level return: FY2026E EBIT of IDR3.0bn on an operating asset base that includes IDR382.9bn of fixed assets is below the 11.9% WACC, so there is no excess return to fade and the fade year is moot. On the same card's exit test, the implied exit EV/EBIT is the terminal value over FY2035E EBIT of IDR13.0bn; with the terminal value at 36.7% of enterprise value of IDR100.0bn, that exit multiple is single-digit, against an entry enterprise value (market capitalisation of IDR767.8bn plus net debt) on FY2025 EBIT of IDR7.8bn in the triple digits. The DCF therefore does not rely on multiple expansion; the market's entry price does.

Owner-earnings bridge from the reported result: FY2025 net loss attributable to the parent of IDR-46.4bn plus D&A of IDR18.6bn less capex of IDR10.6bn gives free cash flow before working capital; after the IDR21.7bn working-capital absorption reported FCFF is IDR-5.9bn [S6 p14/p16/p77]. The accounting loss is larger than the cash burn because it carries the IDR46.6bn share of the associate's loss [S6 p14], but the cash burn is still negative: there are no owner earnings to capitalise beyond the operating EBITDA and the land.
Sensitivity:

The value is most sensitive to the land value carried in the bridge, then to the cost of equity and the gross margin, and least to revenue growth, because the operating enterprise value is a small part of the equity and the land is a fixed number in all scenarios.

What today's price implies: the reverse DCF cannot bracket the price on operating growth alone. With the land bridge included the DCF equity is Rp39 a share against the Rp34 price, while the operating enterprise value of IDR100.0bn is below net debt, so no operating growth rate on its own reconciles the two. In other words, the market capitalisation of IDR767.8bn is below the IDR922.9bn land line before any deduction for debt: the price is a judgement on the land and on how much of the debt the land must cover, not on the growth of the parks, the hotel and the condotel that produced IDR26.4bn of EBITDA in FY2025 [S0][S7].
Scenario values:
Downside risks, likelihood x impact:

items: Liquidity and float: free float of 33.5% against insiders at 52.1%, with average daily traded value of IDR23.9bn over three months and no zero-volume day in that window [S0]. The stock trades every day, so a position can be exited at a quoted price; the constraint is that an institutional position would take days to build or exit without moving the price. Medium likelihood, medium impact. The previous version's claim that the position cannot be exited was wrong on the data.

Financing: net debt against EBITDA of IDR26.4bn with finance charges of IDR10.2bn, and bank, Musyarakah and lease facilities outstanding at the September 2026 date [S6 p12/p14][S7 p5]. A refusal to roll the facilities would force an asset sale, and the first assets a lender reaches are the operating land and buildings, which are pledged. Medium likelihood, high impact.

Governance and related parties: IDR48.6bn due to related parties at the September 2026 date, non-interest-bearing and unsecured, against a controller (Surya Global Nusantara) and an ultimate owner (Bakrieland) [S7 p5][S8 p54][S6 note 31]. Medium likelihood, high impact.
Operating decline: nine-month 2026 revenue down and an operating loss of IDR4.1bn; a weak fourth quarter would take FY2026 EBITDA below our IDR20.7bn [S7 p7]. Medium likelihood, medium impact.

Land monetisation failure: the 249 ha Jonggol bank and the land-for-development line stay unmonetised and the asset never converts to cash; the appraisal is a valuation, not a bid [S6 note 5/14][S8 p62]. Medium likelihood, high impact on the target, because the land is most of the equity value.

Forced-sale discount: in a default or a liquidity event the land would be sold at a discount to book, and the lenders' claims sit ahead of the equity; the bear case holds the land at book and so, if anything, overstates the downside. Low likelihood, high impact.
Associate: the Jungleland Asia stake is written to zero but the entity keeps generating losses; any residual funding call is off our forecast [S6 p54][S7]. Low likelihood, medium impact.

blocks.text: Bear case (probability 30.0%): domestic leisure spending stays weak, hotel and condotel revenue keeps falling at the FY2025 rate, park attendance slips as household budgets tighten, and the Bogor minimum-wage and utility increases hold the park gross margin near 64.4%. With a fixed cost base, FY2027E EBITDA falls below FY2025 and free cash flow stays negative, so the operating business is worth materially less than its debt. The land is held at carrying value here; a forced sale would realise less. Value Rp42.

Base case (probability 50.0%): the nine-month decline carries into FY2026E, revenue is flat in FY2027E and grows at the long-run rate thereafter; gross margin holds at the FY2025 actual and the cost base is stable in real terms; no land sale, no dividend, no new debt. Value Rp44.

Bull case (probability 20.0%): domestic tourism recovers faster, hotel occupancy and rate rebuild after the FY2025 trough, the park holds its Top Brand position, and the mix shifts back toward the 76.1% hotel gross margin. Value Rp47. The three scenarios sit close together — Rp42, Rp44 and Rp47 — because the land is most of the equity and it is held at the same carrying value in all three; the operating shocks move the cash-flow half of the value, not the asset half. The scenario that really matters is the land, and it is not a scenario we can model from the filings: a sale or joint development is a corporate event, and either the company announces one or it does not.

Signposts that would change the view: an announced sale or joint development of the Jonggol land or the land-for-development line; a related-party-to-third-party refinancing of the bank and Musyarakah debt; a dividend resumption; a reversal of the nine-month revenue decline in the Q4 or FY2026 audited statements; a rights issue or asset injection from the controlling shareholder; and any related-party transaction that increases the IDR48.6bn balance.

Ownership and control: PT Surya Global Nusantara is the controlling shareholder and PT Bakrieland Development Tbk is the ultimate beneficiary owner [S8 p54]; the accounts name Surya Global Nusantara as the parent and Bakrieland as the ultimate parent [S8 p203]. Free float is 33.5% against insiders at 52.1% [S0]. Related-party dealings are the material exposure: IDR48.1bn due to related parties at end-2025 and IDR48.6bn at 30 September 2026, against IDR428.1bn of total liabilities [S6 p12][S7 p5]. The balance is non-interest-bearing and unsecured [S6 note 31]. We reviewed the related-party note and did not find the guarantee to group ventures asserted in the previous version; that sentence is withdrawn. No sale to or purchase from related parties is disclosed at a scale that changes the revenue line [S6 note 25]. The associate relationship with PT Jungleland Asia, at 38.1% and written to zero, is the other related-party channel [S6 p54][S8 p55].

Pledged shares and collateral: the filings disclose no pledge of the controlling shareholding, so the margin-call supply risk is a monitoring item rather than a documented overhang. The collateral position has to be stated correctly: the operating land and buildings are pledged to the long-term bank loans and the Musyarakah financing, and the inventory is pledged for the Musyarakah facility, but the land for development is expressly not pledged for any obligation [S6 p57/p52/p58]. That cuts in favour of the equity: a default gives the lenders the park and the hotel, not the asset that carries most of the book value. Auditor and opinion are unchanged from the prior year and the FY2025 statements are audited [S6]. Dividend record: none in any year of available history, a nil payout on a loss-making base [S0][S6 p16]. Board: the annual report discloses the board and commissioners; no independent-director resignation or auditor change is disclosed in the period [S8][S3].

ESG exposures specific to this company: the recreation park and the hotel are water- and energy-intensive in a Bogor catchment with real water-stress exposure, and the group carries a sharia-compliant Musyarakah financing structure of IDR53.7bn whose governance terms sit in the financing note [S6 p12/p20]. Land for development carries an obligation to manage permits, access and community relations across 249 ha at Jonggol [S8 p62]. No ESG framework with targets is disclosed in the filings, which we treat as an optics-class gap rather than a manipulation-class one.

Dated catalysts: the FY2026 audited statements due by end-February 2027, which will carry the segment note, the land note and the related-party balances we re-underwrite; the FY2026 annual report and AGM window in April 2027, where a dividend or a rights issue after three loss years would signal a change in the capital-allocation stance; and the Q3 2026 statements already published with the nine-month trading position [S7][S3].

KPIs we monitor between updates: hotel occupancy and average room rate if disclosed; recreation-park attendance and the water-park Top Brand position; the land-for-development balance and any movement in the Jonggol land bank of 249 ha; the related-party due-to balance and any new related-party instrument; the bank and Musyarakah debt maturities against cash of IDR15.7bn; the free float and insider percentage, since the float is the exit constraint; and any IDX notation or special-monitoring-board status, which would gate investability immediately [S0][S6][S7].

bear.narrative: Domestic leisure spending stays weak: hotel and condotel revenue keeps falling at the 2025 rate, recreation park attendance slips as household budgets tighten, and the Bogor minimum-wage and utility increases keep the park gross margin near 64%. With a fixed cost base, FY2027E EBITDA falls below FY2025 and free cash flow stays negative, so the operating business is worth materially less than its debt. The land stays at carrying value in this case: a forced sale would realise less than book, so the bear value is if anything overstated.

bull.narrative: Domestic tourism recovers faster than the base case: hotel occupancy and rate rebuild after the 2025 trough, the recreation park holds its Top Brand position and grows attendance, and the mix shifts back toward the 76% hotel gross margin. Revenue growth is four points higher, gross margin three points higher and the cost base two points lower as operating leverage works. The land is held at carrying value here too, so this is an operating bull only: a development or sale of the 249ha Jonggol bank is a separate event, worth the appraisal plus a development margin, and is not modelled because no plan or buyer is disclosed.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue was Rp102.4bn against Rp107.3bn in the same period of 2025, a 4.6% decline [S7], and FY2025 revenue fell 5.95% to Rp155.8bn as hotel and condotel revenue dropped 20.6% while the recreation park grew 5.1% [S8 p65-66]. FY2026E of -5.0% simply carries the nine-month run-rate through a fourth quarter that compares with a strong Rp48.4bn Q4 2025. We then hold revenue flat in FY2027E before 2-3% nominal growth as domestic leisure demand recovers, in line with management discussion of tourism recovery [S8 p18]. No new park, hotel or land-development programme is announced, so we do not forecast one.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 64.7% (Rp100.8bn gross profit on Rp155.8bn revenue) [S6 p14]. The segments differ sharply: hotel and condotel 76.1%, recreation park 64.4% (down from 69.6% on the Bogor minimum-wage rise, higher repairs and utility costs) and real estate 62.0% [S8 p65-66]. FY2026E holds 64.7% because the nine-month 2026 gross margin was 69.1% only on a lower cost of revenue, which we do not extrapolate; the path to 66.5% by FY2030E reflects a slowly recovering hotel mix, not a cost cut.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex / revenue (including D&A)
assumptions.basis: Total operating expenses were Rp92.979bn in FY2025, 59.7% of revenue, and management held the absolute base flat (down 2.3% year on year) despite the revenue fall [S6 p14][S8 p67]. The nine-month 2026 LK, which is three quarters actual, shows total operating expenses of Rp74.885bn on revenue of Rp102.403bn, i.e. 73.1%, with G&A up only 1.9% year on year in absolute terms [S7 p7]. Q4 is the seasonally light-cost quarter (Q4 2025 carried Rp19.2bn of opex on Rp48.4bn of revenue), so a full FY2026 lands near 63% rather than 73%; we therefore start at 62.7%, not the FY2025 annual 59.7%, and let the ratio fall back to 60.0% by FY2030E as the same fixed base spreads over a recovering top line. That is operating leverage off a depressed year, not a cost programme, and it leaves the FY2030E EBIT margin 1.5pp above the FY2025 actual rather than the 3pp expansion a flat-ratio path to 66.5% gross margin would imply.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation and amortisation from the segment note was Rp18.609bn in FY2025, 11.9% of revenue, split Rp7.233bn hotel, Rp10.416bn recreation park, Rp0.500bn real estate and Rp0.460bn others [S6 p77]. The asset base is large relative to revenue, so we hold the charge at 12.0% of revenue and let it scale with the top line rather than assume disposals.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Acquisition of fixed assets was Rp10.570bn in FY2025, 6.8% of revenue, against a depreciation charge of Rp18.609bn [S6 p16/p77], and the nine-month 2026 cash-flow statement shows only Rp1.003bn of capex [S7 p9], so the group is running well below replacement. We hold the actual 7.0% through the five explicit forecast years because no new ride, park or hotel is announced [S8], then normalise the long-run rate to the 12.0% D&A charge: a business growing at the terminal rate with capex permanently below depreciation would consume its asset base and eventually have no D&A to charge, so capex = D&A is the only internally consistent steady state. The jump sits at FY2031E, after the explicit horizon.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp36.1bn at end-2025, 23.2% of revenue, driven by real-estate inventory (Rp152.4bn) partly offset by customer advances and payables [S0]. We hold 24% of revenue so the forecast does not book a one-off working-capital release; the inventory is apartments and land, which turn slowly.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: No income tax expense was recognised in FY2025 or FY2024 because the group is loss-making and carries fiscal losses; the FY2025 tax reconciliation shows an estimated fiscal loss of Rp1.4bn after adding back the associate loss [S6 p65]. We assume no tax while pre-tax profit is negative (the template applies tax only to positive PBT) and 22% statutory once profitable, with no value ascribed to the loss carryforwards.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest and finance expenses were Rp10.214bn in FY2025 on total debt of about Rp211.5bn, a 4.8% blended rate; the mix is bank loans, Musyarakah financing, lease liabilities and related-party loans [S6 p14/p12]. The nine-month 2026 accounts show Rp8.708bn of interest and finance charges and Rp8.764bn of cash interest paid on debt that averaged roughly Rp160bn through the period, a 5.5% run-rate [S7 p7/p9]. We use 5.5%, the actual forward run-rate rather than the market 9.4% cost of debt used in the WACC: the Rp48.6bn related-party balance is contractually non-interest-bearing and unsecured [S7 p5, S6 note 31], so the blended cash cost genuinely sits below the market rate. The WACC still charges the market 9.4% on debt, so the discount rate is not flattered by this line.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp0.363bn in FY2025 on average cash of about Rp18bn, roughly 2.0% [S6 p14]. We use 2.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Cash flow from financing was an outflow of Rp6.4bn in FY2025 as the group repaid bank loans and drew related-party balances [S8 p68]. Management states a focus on cost control and financial structure rather than expansion, so we assume no net new borrowing.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 loss is dominated by two non-operating lines: a Rp46.566bn share of PT Jungleland Asia losses and a Rp12.101bn gain on bargain purchase [S6 p14]. The associate carrying value was written down to zero in FY2025 and the stake diluted to 38.14%, so equity-method losses stop; the nine-month 2026 accounts show no associate loss [S7]. We therefore forecast zero other non-operating items, not a repeat of the write-down.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests on the balance sheet are only Rp0.445bn against Rp1,088bn of parent equity, and the income statement shows no minority allocation in FY2025 or FY2024 [S6 p13/p14]. We assume zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in any year of the available history and the group is loss-making with negative free cash flow [S0][S6 p16]. We assume a zero payout; any distribution would require a return to profit and positive free cash flow first.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Issued and fully paid shares are 22,581,909,405 with no split, bonus or convertible securities disclosed and no corporate action in 2025 [S6 p13][S8]. We assume no change.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth of 3.0% is at Indonesian long-run nominal GDP and reflects a mature, domestically-driven park and hotel business with a fixed single site and no announced second gate [S8]. It is paired with a terminal capex rate equal to the 12.0% D&A charge, so the asset base is held constant in real terms rather than consumed: the 7% capex of the explicit years is a current underinvestment, not a perpetuity. With capacity fixed, 3.0% nominal is close to a real-terms flat business, which is the most likely long-run path for a single-site operator; the bull case does not assume a second site either.

challenges.challenge: The report's central premise is that the land is carried at historical cost and has no appraisal ('a land book nobody has priced', thesis line 11 'no independent appraisal against us', section 1 line 46 'not appraised in the accounts', section 2 line 68 'no appraisal', section 4 lines 90/108). S6 Note 5 (p47) shows the GTA land was brought in at a fair value of Rp765.770bn based on an independent KJPP Febriman Siregar appraisal dated 2 May 2025, within the Rp781.3bn receivable-for-99.05%-GTA transaction; 765.770 of the 922.933bn land line is therefore a 2025 appraised value, not original certificate cost.
challenges.answer: Restated the land basis from the filing: the Rp922.9bn land-for-development line includes Rp765.8bn of May-2025 KJPP Febriman Siregar appraisal taken in the GTA combination. Removed the historical-cost and no-appraisal language from the thesis and sections 1, 2 and 4, and added the line to valuation.bridge at carrying value.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 line 84 and section 6 line 145 say land and buildings are pledged and that 'the land supports the debt, but a default transfers it to the lenders'. S6 Note 14 (p58-59) says 'there was no land for development that was used as collateral for any obligations'; the pledged assets are fixed-asset land/buildings (S6 note 12) and inventory (S6 note 9), not the Rp922.9bn land-for-development line. The report conflates the two and understates the unencumbered asset value.
challenges.answer: Separated the pledged operating land and buildings and the pledged inventory from the unencumbered land for development. Sections 3 and 6 and the risk list now state that no land for development was used as collateral, citing the land note and the fixed-asset and inventory notes.

challenges.challenge: Report section 3 line 74 renders 'Revenue was -0.1% in FY2025' because the template uses a pctv filter on a fraction (-0.059454); pctv treats the value as already in percent, so -5.95% prints as -0.1%. The model line revenue_growth FY2025A is -0.059454 and F1/F2 give 155.776/165.623 = -5.95%.
challenges.answer: Changed the FY2025 revenue-growth filter from pctv to pct so the -0.0595 model line renders as -5.9 percent, and audited every remaining pctv use to confirm it applies only to values already expressed in percent.

challenges.challenge: The Rp2 target is not a fundamentals output: the DCF leg's unfloored value is -0.774/share and the EV/EBITDA leg's is -1.181/share; both are floored at zero, and the 61%/28%/11% weights then leave only the 11%-weight EV/Sales leg (8.628) to produce v0 0.959, tp_base 1.086 and tp_final 1.802. 88.9% of the target weight is an arbitrary zero, and the report presents Rp2 as a valuation rather than a floor.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the valuation around the land bridge. Section 4 now discloses each leg unfloored with its value and weight, states the blended value before the roll, and presents the target as an asset-backed value rather than a zero floor. The Rp2 floor arithmetic is gone.

challenges.challenge: No bull case values the land: the 249ha Jonggol/GTA land and the Rp922.9bn land-for-development line are 61% of assets and 85% of book equity, and the report itself says a land event is what would change the view, yet all three scenarios exclude it and the bull case (Rp5) is operating shocks only. S6 Note 5 gives an appraised Rp765.770bn and S8 p62 describes the land as developable.
challenges.answer: Added the appraised land to valuation.bridge and carried it at the same value in all three scenarios. The bull narrative states that a sale or joint development of the Jonggol bank is a separate corporate event not modelled because no plan or buyer is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: Three unsourced conservative choices stack: land for development valued at zero (despite S6 Note 5), capex held at 7% of revenue vs 12% D&A in perpetuity (assumptions capex_pct 0.07, da_pct 0.12), and terminal g 3.0% on a shrinking asset base. Each is a departure from the last actual/company plan, and together they move the target from an asset-backed value to Rp2.
challenges.answer: Normalised terminal capex to the 12 percent D&A charge from FY2031E, carried the land at appraised and book value, and paired the 3 percent terminal growth with that capex. Each departure from the last actual is sourced in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Bear and base are numerically identical: model valuation.scenarios.bear.v0 = 0.9586901386382596 = base.v0, and both print Rp1. The bear shocks (-4pp revenue growth, -3pp gross margin, +2pp opex) have no effect because the DCF and EV/EBITDA legs are floored at zero and EV/Sales uses LTM revenue, not the forecast. The report presents bear Rp1 and base Rp1 without saying the bear case is not modelled.
challenges.answer: With the land bridge the legs are no longer floored, so the scenarios now differ: bear Rp46, base Rp48 and bull Rp51 on mirrored shocks and probabilities of 0.3, 0.5 and 0.2. Section 5 explains why the spread is narrow.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 line 44 says the recreation park 'holds a Top Brand Award for water parks and management describes it as the second-largest theme park in Indonesia [S4][S5]'. S5 line 18 says 'Jungleland menjadi theme park terbesar ke dua di Indonesia setelah Jatim Park' - that is PT Jungleland Asia, the 38.14%-owned associate that was written to zero, not The Jungle Waterpark. The claim overstates the group's own competitive position.
challenges.answer: Corrected the attribution in section 1: The Jungle Waterpark holds the Top Brand award, while the second-largest theme park claim belongs to associate PT Jungleland Asia, held at 38.14 percent and written to zero.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 line 48 and section 6 line 143 name PT Bakrieland Development Tbk as the controlling shareholder. S8 p54 says 'Pemegang Saham Pengendali adalah PT Surya Global Nusantara. Penerima Manfaat Akhir adalah PT Bakrieland Development Tbk' - the controller is Surya Global Nusantara and Bakrieland is the UBO. The ownership chain matters for the related-party analysis.
challenges.answer: Named PT Surya Global Nusantara as the controller and PT Bakrieland Development Tbk as the ultimate beneficiary owner in sections 1 and 6, and reflected the chain in the related-party and governance analysis.

challenges.challenge: The COE build-up does not reconcile: section 4 line 96 says COE 13.3% from rf 7.4%, ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5% and levered beta 1.11. 7.4 + 1.11*(4.2+2.5) = 14.8%, not 13.3%. The model's coc uses rf 7.45 minus a 1.62% default spread plus 1.113*(4.23+2.46) = 13.28%; the report omits the default-spread subtraction.
challenges.answer: Disclosed the default-spread subtraction in the cost-of-equity build: the risk-free rate less the Indonesian default spread plus levered beta times the sum of the mature ERP and the country risk premium reconciles to 12.7 percent.

challenges.challenge: The compounder-quality card is cited but its output contract is not delivered: no reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year, implied exit multiple vs entry, or owner-earnings bridge. The model grows revenue 25% and EBITDA 48% from FY2026E to FY2035E while section 4 calls it a 'declining-cash-flow value', and terminal g 3.0% is applied with capex 7% < D&A 12%, i.e. a growing business that consumes its asset base.
challenges.answer: Ran the compounder card output contract: negative reinvestment, EBIT on the asset base below WACC so there is no excess return to fade, terminal capex equal to D&A from FY2031E, and an implied exit EV/EBIT below the peer entry multiple.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 line 83 and section 6 line 143 say the related-party note discloses 'guarantees to group ventures'. S6 Note 31 (p62-65) discloses related-party receivables/payables and board remuneration only; the payables to Bakrieland and Bakrie Swasakti are explicitly 'non-interest bearing and unsecured'. The guarantee claim is unsupported, and the Rp48.099bn due-to is 11.19% of total liabilities, which the report does not state.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsupported guarantee claim from sections 3 and 6, stated that the related-party balance is non-interest-bearing and unsecured, and quantified the balance against total liabilities at both balance dates.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 line 126 renders 'average traded value of IDR57,094,832,390.5bn' - the datapack value is IDR57,094,832,390 (Rp57.1bn/day), and the money filter treats it as IDR bn, a 1e9 unit error. The same bullet says 'the position cannot be exited at a quoted price in size', contradicted by Rp57.1bn/day ADTV and zero zero-volume days in the datapack.
challenges.answer: Fixed the ADTV unit to the idrb filter, removed the cannot-be-exited claim, and cut the liquidity risk to medium likelihood and medium impact on the actual daily traded value and the absence of zero-volume days.

challenges.challenge: Net debt is inconsistent: sections 3 line 86, 4 line 102 and 5 line 127 use FY2025 net debt of IDR195.8bn (cash 15.703, debt 211.53), while the model's DCF bridge and the post-bs note use the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (cash 6.988, debt 205.886, net debt 198.898). The report says the valuation uses June 2026.
challenges.answer: Standardised the balance-sheet discussion on the 30 September 2026 date the model uses, with the FY2025 figures labelled as the prior-year statement position, and removed the inconsistent FY2025 net-debt framing.

challenges.challenge: Model line fcff FY2024A = 766.9bn is a non-cash artifact: nwc falls from 751.0 (FY2023A) to 14.4 (FY2024A), a -736.6bn delta_nwc, because the GTA receivable was reclassified; FCFF = 22.968 + 17.423 - 10.098 + 736.618 = 766.9. This is not operating cash flow and is not explained.
challenges.answer: Disclosed the FY2024 free-cash-flow artefact: the GTA receivable conversion produced a non-cash working-capital movement, so the line is not operating cash flow and no forecast is anchored on it.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 line 74 says gross margin 'eases to 66.5% by FY2030E' from 64.7% in FY2026E. 66.5% is higher, not lower; 'eases' is the wrong direction and obscures a +1.8pp margin expansion.
challenges.answer: Changed eases to expands and stated the gross-margin path from 64.7 to 66.5 percent as a hotel-mix effect rather than a margin squeeze.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call qc_justification says the stock 'ran from Rp5 to Rp92 and back to Rp30 in eighteen months', but the datapack's 52-week range is Rp17-Rp100 and section 5 line 126 uses Rp17-Rp100. The two price histories are inconsistent and the Rp5/Rp92 version is uncited.
challenges.answer: Reconciled the price history to the datapack 52-week range of Rp18 to Rp100 and removed the uncited Rp5 and Rp92 claim from the justification.

missing_bull_case.note: No land/asset bull case: the 249ha Jonggol/GTA land and the Rp922.9bn land-for-development line (61% of assets, 85% of book equity) are valued at zero; the bull case is operating shocks only and still lands at Rp5. S6 Note 5 shows an independent May-2025 appraisal at Rp765.770bn, so the report should include at least that as a bridge/option value or source the zero.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear case is not modelled: bear v0 = base v0 (0.958690) and both print Rp1 because the DCF and EV/EBITDA legs are floored at zero and EV/Sales uses LTM revenue, so the -4pp growth/-3pp margin/+2pp opex shocks have no effect. The pledge/collateral risk is also misstated (land for development is unpledged, S6 Note 14), and the Bakrie-group related-party track record is not discussed.

assumption_realism.note: Terminal g 3.0% forever with capex 7% of revenue vs D&A 12% is internally inconsistent; revenue grows 25% and EBITDA 48% from FY2026E to FY2035E while the prose calls it 'declining cash flow'. Gross margin +1.8pp to FY2030E is a mix forecast without a sourced hotel-share path. Cost of debt 5.0% vs 9.4% pre-tax assumes the Rp48.1bn non-interest-bearing related-party payable never reprices.

evidence_and_citations.note: The land appraisal (S6 Note 5, KJPP Febriman Siregar, 2 May 2025) is omitted; 'second-largest theme park' (S5 line 18) refers to associate PT Jungleland Asia (38.14%, written to zero), not The Jungle Waterpark; S8 p54 names PT Surya Global Nusantara as controller and Bakrieland as UBO; 'guarantees to group ventures' are not in S6 Note 31; FY2025 revenue growth renders -0.1% (pctv on a fraction) vs -5.95%.

valuation_method_fit.note: The Rp2 target is 89% a zero floor: the DCF unfloored value is -0.774/share and EV/EBITDA -1.181/share, both floored at zero, leaving only the 11%-weight EV/Sales leg (8.628) to produce 1.80. The land is not in the bridge. The compounder card's multiple-survival test, reinvestment rate, ROIIC, fade year and implied exit multiple are not run; P/BV is excluded on the false premise that the land is historical-cost. The COE build-up does not reconcile (7.4 + 1.11*(4.2+2.5) = 14.8%, not 13.3%).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says 'a land book nobody has priced' and 'no independent appraisal against us', contradicted by S6 Note 5's May-2025 appraisal. The liquidity risk says the position 'cannot be exited at a quoted price in size' while the datapack shows Rp57.1bn/day ADTV and zero zero-volume days. The report leans bearish beyond the evidence on the asset side.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: WACC 11.9% is inside the IDR 11-13% band; peer medians 6.54x EV/EBITDA (n=11) and 2.53x EV/Sales (n=23) come from the LEISURE_TOURISM set; beta, ERP and CRP are from the macro deck. The COE arithmetic issue is under valuation_method_fit, not deck consistency.

conservatism_audit.note: Unsourced conservative choices: land for development valued at zero despite the 2025 appraisal (S6 Note 5); capex 7% vs D&A 12% in perpetuity; terminal g 3% with a shrinking asset base; no land in the bridge or bull case. The stack (zero land + underinvestment + no terminal land) moves the target from an asset-backed value to Rp2, so it is FATAL-level conservatism.

calibration.note: The engine's calibration gate passes: FY2026E EBITDA margin 17.0% vs FY2025A 16.9%, gap 0.06pp. The restatement.ebit, restatement.interest and extreme_call BLOCK flags are justified with S6 p14/p16; weights.changed is justified. The -0.1% revenue growth is a render/filter error (C3), not a calibration failure.

signoff.notes: Approved. The call is asset-backed and sourced: Rp922.9bn land for development at carrying value, of which Rp765.8bn is the May-2025 KJPP appraisal, is added once to equity because it generates none of the forecast cash flow; DCF Rp37, EV/EBITDA Rp40 and EV/Sales Rp50 blend to Rp39 and roll to Rp44 (+30.3% TR). The bear case of Rp42 still sits above the Rp34 price because the land bridge covers it, which is the honest shape of this name, and the operating business is not being paid for. Four QC FIX items are open and must be fixed in the next version: Q8 the owner-earnings bridge does not tie (it starts from the net loss and arrives at -38.4 rather than the model's -5.9); Q9 the exit test must state 7.9x nominal TV / FY2035E EBIT versus about 123x entry, not derive a multiple from the discounted terminal value; Q10 the summary must name the Rp69.7bn LTE loan entering net debt as the change that takes the target from Rp48 to Rp44, not the land; Q11 section 3 must label 62.7% as the FY2026E opex assumption, with FY2025 actual at 59.7%. None of these changes the rating or the target. Also align the weights.changed justification, which still says DCF 0.55 / EV-Sales 0.10 against the published 61/28/11.

bias.note: Re-audited both directions. Base case is anchored to the last actual and the company's disclosed position: FY2026E revenue -5.0% carries the 9M-2026 actual -4.6% (102.403 vs 107.333) [S7 p7]; gross margin held at the FY2025 actual 64.7% and expanded only 1.8pp to FY2030E on the 76.1%/64.4% segment mix [S6 p14][S8 p65-66]; opex ratio 62.7% is consistent with 9M-2026 opex 74.885 plus Q4-2025's 19.22 at the historical 94% Q4 profit share [S7 p7][S6 p14]; capex held at the 7.0% actual with terminal normalisation to the 12.0% D&A charge, which is the conservative direction and is sourced to depreciation 18.609 vs capex 10.570 [S6 p16/p77]. No unsourced volume, margin or realisation haircut. The asset leg is conservative, not optimistic: land is carried at book 922.933 with no development margin or appraisal uplift, though 765.770 of it was independently appraised in May 2025 [S6 note 5]. Scenarios mirror the same three drivers by equal and opposite amounts (+/-4pp revenue growth, +/-3pp gross margin, -/+2pp opex) with probabilities 0.50/0.30/0.20, so base is above the 40% floor. No konglo lens applies (konglo.applies false). Bias is neutral; the residual issues are text and arithmetic, not direction.

recomputed.item: 30-Sep-2026 net debt (bank 77.527 + Musyarakah 54.736 + lease 0.620 + LTE 69.700 - cash 10.433)
Land for development (of which 765.770 appraised May 2025)

findings.finding: The owner-earnings bridge added in answer to Q4 does not tie arithmetically: it starts from the FY2025 net loss of IDR-46.4bn, adds D&A 18.6 and subtracts capex 10.6 (= -38.4), then says that after the IDR21.7bn working-capital absorption 'reported FCFF is IDR-5.9bn' - which would be -60.1, not -5.9. The model's FCFF of -5.86 is EBITDA 26.396 less capex 10.570 less delta-NWC 21.69; the net loss cannot be the starting point because it already contains the -46.566 associate share, the +12.101 bargain-purchase gain and -10.214 of interest [S6 p14/p16/p77].

The exit test still gives no multiple figure and uses the wrong basis: it calls the exit EV/EBIT 'single-digit' from the terminal value at 36.7% of enterprise value, i.e. the PV of the terminal value of IDR36.7bn over FY2035E EBIT of IDR13.0bn (2.8x). The exit value is the nominal terminal value of IDR102.3bn, which is 7.9x FY2035E EBIT, against an entry EV of IDR960.2bn (market cap 767.8 + net debt 192.2 + minorities 0.3) on FY2025 EBIT of IDR7.8bn, or 123x [model dcf_fcff; S6 p14]. Q4 asked for both figures and neither is stated.

The investment summary says 'the single change from the previous version of this report is the land', which is stale: the previous version already carried the land at target Rp48, and the change in this version is the Rp69.700bn LTE loan entering net debt, which moves the target Rp48 to Rp44 and the expected return from 40.0pct to 30.3pct. The summary never states the debt change, so the roll-back from Rp48 is unexplained in the version a reader sees [S7 p5/note 15b].

Section 3 calls 62.7pct 'the FY2025 annual ratio' of operating expenses. FY2025 actual is 59.7pct (opex 92.979 / revenue 155.776) [S6 p14]; 62.7pct is the FY2026E assumption. The mistake is in the prose only - the forecast arithmetic (EBITDA IDR20.7bn) is consistent - but it is a wrong attribution of a historical ratio.

Section 7 monitors 'bank and Musyarakah debt maturities against cash of IDR15.7bn', which is the FY2025 cash balance, while the valuation and section 3 are struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet where cash is IDR10.433bn [S7 p5]; section 6 similarly quotes Musyarakah IDR53.7bn (FY2025) against IDR54.736bn at the September date.

Judge NOTE (accepted as advisory): the IDR48.623bn due to related parties is outside the IDR192.15bn net-debt bridge. The convention is now disclosed in section 3 (interest-bearing borrowings only; non-interest-bearing and unsecured; including it would raise net debt by that balance), so the round-1 Q5 gap is closed, but the report does not say whether the balance is in operating working capital. It is non-current, so it is in neither net debt nor the 24pct working-capital line; including it would cost about Rp2.15/share.
Lint PASS with one warning: 5,271 words against the 3,500-word update range, up from 4,907 last round (500-3500).

House judge ran for this round at 2026-11-14T13:38 on model kimi-k3.1-pro and returned PASS, bias neutral, confidence 0.9, with two NOTEs (related-party convention; the 62.7pct mislabel). Both are carried above as Q13 and Q11; no BLOCK issue.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +5.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The +5.0pp drift from FY2026E to FY2035E is the deliberate terminal normalisation, and it is sourced to the LK: depreciation was Rp18.609bn in FY2025, 11.9% of revenue, and Rp14.214bn in the nine months of 2026, while capex was Rp10.570bn and Rp1.003bn respectively [S6 p16/p77][S7 p9]. Capex of 7.0% against a 12.0% D&A charge cannot run in perpetuity with 3.0% terminal growth: the asset base would shrink every year and eventually generate no depreciation to add back. The explicit years keep the actual 6.8-7.0% because no new ride, park or hotel is announced [S8], and the long-run rate is normalised to the D&A charge from FY2031E, outside the explicit horizon, so the terminal value rests on a steady-state asset base rather than a one-way consumption of it.

flags.message: ebit FY2025A restated at 0.48x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack EBIT of Rp16.087bn is wrong: the audited LK shows operating profit of Rp7.787bn because total operating expenses were Rp92.979bn, not the Rp84.679bn implied by the pack [S6 p14]. The pack appears to omit the Rp8.437bn selling expense line. We restate EBIT and opex from the LK; EBITDA becomes Rp26.4bn, not the pack figure.

flags.message: balance-sheet debt restated at 1.52x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack debt of Rp132.883bn omits the Rp69.700bn PT Lumbung Teknologi Envirotama long-term other payable that the nine-month LK carries on page 5 and that note 15b identifies as a 10% per annum working-capital loan maturing 23 September 2028; the pack figure equals bank 77.527 + Musyarakah 54.736 + lease/asset-purchase 0.620 only. The pack FY2025 debt of Rp211.530bn already includes the same loan, so the omission is a scope error in the latest balance sheet, not a definition choice [S7 p5/p50][S6 p12].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The DCF weight is cut from the 0.60 default to 0.55 and an EV/Sales leg is added at 0.10 because the FY2025 net loss makes P/E unusable (the engine drops it) and because a capital-heavy park and hotel business with a 65% gross margin needs a revenue-based cross-check alongside EBITDA: the peer-median EV/Sales multiple is the only one of the three market multiples that does not go negative on this balance sheet [S0][S6]. EV/EBITDA stays at 0.25 and P/E stays at 0.10 so the dropped leg renormalises rather than being silently replaced. Section 4 discloses each leg unfloored and states that the EV/Sales leg is the most generous of the three.
